analysis.one_liner: Bans deductibles on outpatient pediatric care in private insurance, Medicaid, CHIP, and TRICARE.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a single cosponsor, never received a committee vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred health plans from applying a deductible to outpatient care for children under 18, including care delivered by telehealth. That would have meant first-dollar coverage for pediatric doctor visits, therapies, and other outpatient services in employer plans, individual market plans, Medicaid, CHIP, and TRICARE. The bill never got past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, especially those in high-deductible health plans who currently pay the full cost of pediatric outpatient visits until meeting a deductible. The bill also included a tax-code fix so plans could drop the pediatric deductible without disqualifying families from health savings account eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children on high-deductible plans

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits group health plans, individual and group insurance issuers, Medicaid, CHIP, and TRICARE from applying a deductible to outpatient pediatric services furnished to anyone under 18, in person or by telehealth [S2][S3].

It applies across four statutes — ERISA, the Public Health Service Act, the Internal Revenue Code, and the Social Security Act — plus TRICARE, so the ban reaches employer plans, individual market plans, public programs, and military families [S3].

The bill adds a safe harbor so a plan dropping the pediatric deductible does not fail to qualify as a high-deductible health plan, which would otherwise jeopardize health savings account eligibility for those families [S3].
It directs the Comptroller General to report within four years on how the change affected premiums, deductibles, and copayments, and gives plans and programs two years to comply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans would absorb the cost of first-dollar pediatric coverage, and that cost would likely be passed back into higher premiums for all enrollees; Medicaid, CHIP, and TRICARE would bear added federal and state costs.

drawbacks.text: Banning deductibles for outpatient pediatric care shifts those costs into premiums or public spending for everyone, not just families using pediatric care; the bill's own GAO study provision anticipates effects on premiums, deductibles, and copayments [S3].

The definition is broad — any item or service furnished to a person under 18 as an outpatient — so it would extend first-dollar coverage well beyond routine pediatric visits to high-cost outpatient services as well [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families facing pediatric deductibles is real and targeted, and the bill sensibly included the HSA safe harbor and a compliance runway. The tradeoff is higher premiums or program costs spread across all enrollees and taxpayers, and the bill offered no offset to pay for the Medicaid, CHIP, and TRICARE changes. On balance a modest, focused consumer benefit, but never tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, and none of them ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier introduced the bill on October 9, 2020, near the end of the 116th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and additionally to Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Armed Services [S5].
No committee reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred; its last recorded action is the October 9, 2020 referral [S5].
It drew a single cosponsor, a House Democrat, and no further action followed [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and employers keep collecting pediatric deductibles, and taxpayers avoid the added Medicaid, CHIP, and TRICARE cost — families with high-deductible coverage gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers, not pediatric families

sides.party_line_note: The bill was too early in its life to draw opposition: it had one Democratic cosponsor and no vote ever occurred, so no party split is visible.

industries.note: The bill would end insurers' ability to apply deductibles to outpatient pediatric care, eliminating cost-sharing revenue on that care and pushing its costs into premiums. Its interest in the bill's failure ran against families who pay pediatric deductibles.
Self-insured employer plans are covered by the ERISA provision, so employers would bear the added cost of first-dollar pediatric coverage, likely through higher premium contributions.
First-dollar coverage removes a financial barrier that causes families to delay pediatric visits, increasing demand for outpatient pediatric services. Their interest runs alongside families'.
